Further screening of genes identified in single cell atlases as being enriched in IPCs led to the identification of numerous genes that function in IPCs to regulate sleep, including modulators of wnt and insulin signaling. Together, these findings identify a fat body-IPC axis that is a critical modulator of sleep duration and intensity.

articles.titulo: Class-wide sequence, structural, and docking-profile diversity of insect odorant receptors and structural specialization of Orco.
articles.autores: Zhang T, Yang X, Fu Y, Xue W, Zhang Y, Duan S, Yin Y, Guo Y, Gao C, Liu Y, Li G, Xu C, Lu H
articles.resumo_original: Insect olfaction is facilitated by a heterotetrameric odorant receptor-odorant receptor co-receptor (OR-Orco) complex. However, extensive sequence divergence and lineage-specific expansion have complicated large-scale comparisons of OR repertoires across insects. Here, we integrated sequence similarity, structural similarity, and molecular docking to analyze ORs from 115 insect species. OR repertoire size was associated with adult diet, larval diet, and habitat, but not with circadian rhythm. We developed a 'trunk-branch' network framework to classify ORs according to sequence and structural similarity and used large-scale molecular docking to derive comparative docking profiles. Despite marked differences in sequence- and structural-community composition, almost all sampled orders contained ORs assigned to all six docking-profile communities. Holometabolous insects showed higher OR sequence-community diversity than non-holometabolous insects, and docking-profile composition differed between extant lineages whose order-level origins predate or postdate the end-Permian mass extinction. Most notably, we identified a highly conserved extracellular β-sheet in Orco that restricts ligand access to the binding pocket and may contribute to its reduced capacity to bind natural odorants. The emergence of Orco represents a key evolutionary transition from homomeric receptors to heteromeric OR-Orco complexes, and our results suggest that this transition may have been accompanied by pronounced specialization of the extracellular domain and binding pocket. Together, these analyses provide a class-wide framework for comparing insect OR diversity and generate testable hypotheses for future experimental and evolutionary studies.

articles.titulo: Conservation of a synaptic blueprint across the animal kingdom.
articles.autores: Houcek AJ, Kavalali ET
articles.resumo_original: Chemical synapses are fundamental computational units of the nervous system that enable rapid and precise information transfer through the nanoscale organization of presynaptic and postsynaptic components. Despite hundreds of millions of years of animal evolution and extraordinary diversity in nervous system architectures, the core physiological principles of chemical synaptic transmission remain remarkably conserved. Studies across Drosophila melanogaster, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, frogs and mammals reveal recurring principles governing active-zone organization, synaptic vesicle exocytosis, calcium signalling and postsynaptic specialization. Here, we examine the evolution of chemical synapses across the animal kingdom, focusing on the relationship between molecular diversification, nanoscale organization and functional conservation. We propose that the evolutionary stability of synapses reflects, in part, a stringent biophysical constraint imposed by the requirements for rapid chemical communication. We further consider how these conserved synaptic operations are assembled into neural circuits of dramatically different complexities, as well as the ctenophore nervous system as a critical test case for distinguishing molecular conservation from architectural and functional convergence. Across species, the emerging picture is that evolution has adhered to conserving the geometry and organizational principles of chemical synapses more stringently than a precise molecular composition. Synapses thus represent stable yet adaptable information-processing architectures in which conserved nanoscale constraints coexist with molecular flexibility and extensive diversification of neural circuits.

articles.titulo: Advances in research on the regulation of honey bee odor and chemical communication by symbiotic microorganisms.
articles.autores: Chen YJ, Wang YC, Pang YT, Fang RC, Zhang J, Ke XH, Li JJ, Zhang LS, Yang S, Guo J, Miao CH
articles.resumo_original: Because honey bees are key pollinators in terrestrial ecosystems, they are highly sensitive to environmental changes, and colony survival serves as a reliable indicator of environmental conditions. Insect symbiotic microorganisms regulate host chemical communication through multiple pathways, thereby playing critical roles in pheromone synthesis, olfactory perception, and social behavior modulation. However, a systematic review of the potential regulatory mechanisms by which symbiotic microorganisms influence chemical communication in honey bees is still lacking. Here, we synthesize domestic and international research to assess the compositions of symbiotic microorganisms in honey bees, as well as the mechanisms of pheromone release, perception, and function. Furthermore, drawing on specific experimental cases, we discuss how honey bee symbionts modulate host sensitivity to chemical signals and consequently affect host social behavior through multiple routes. These pathways are involved in regulating odorant-binding protein or odorant receptor expression and nervous system function, altering cuticular hydrocarbon profiles, modulating olfactory memory, and mediating immune signaling. This review further explores the interplay between symbiotic microorganisms and the release and reception of chemical signals in honey bees, thereby providing a solid foundation for the conservation of endangered pollinating insects.

articles.titulo: Olfactory differences among cactophilic Drosophila species.
articles.revista: Journal of comparative physiology. A, Neuroethology, sensory, neural, and behavioral physiology
articles.autores: Hamrick A, Layne JE, Lawson LP, Solomon N, Rollmann SM
articles.resumo_original: Divergence of behavioral traits with adaptation to changes in the environment has been well documented in many animals and is often accompanied by divergence in sensory systems. Shifts in insect host plant preference behavior, in particular, are often associated with changes to the olfactory system, including differences in the sensitivity, specificity, or abundance of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs). Here, we examine 12 species from the cactophilic Drosophila repleta group that represent three broad host-use categories: Opuntia specialists, columnar cactus specialists, and polymorphic species that use both host types. We recorded odor-evoked responses from all six maxillary palp OSN classes using single sensillum recordings and used electropalpograms to further evaluate species in which a pb2B-like class was not detected by single sensillum recordings (SSRs). The B-neuron classes clustered largely by OSN identity across species, retaining characteristic class-specific response profiles. The A-neuron classes were less clearly separated because of weak or overlapping response profiles. Despite these shared class-specific responses, species differed substantially in response magnitude and sensitivity to odorants. A pb2B-like class was not detected by SSR in D. mulleri, D. aldrichi, and D. straubae. Electropalpograms supported the absence or strong reduction of a phenol-responsive palpal signal in D. mulleri and D. straubae, while D. aldrichi retained a strong response. Principal component and phylogenetic principal component analyses did not reveal consistent clustering by host-use category. These results suggest that maxillary palp olfaction has evolved in a species- or lineage-specific manner rather than through a repeated host-category-specific shift in peripheral sensitivity.

articles.titulo: Clock neurons modulate seizure timing through a diurnal switch.
articles.autores: Cuddapah VA, Hsu CT, Pant C, Guevara C, Yang J, Killiany S, Shah HM, Putt ME, Sehgal A
articles.resumo_original: People with epilepsy experience daily oscillations in seizure risk. Using a video-tracking model to automate detection, we explored mechanisms underlying spontaneous seizures in Drosophila and find that flies, like people, exhibit daily oscillations in seizure risk. These rhythms are absent in flies lacking a molecular circadian clock and are independent of sleep. Thermogenetic screening and cell-specific clock perturbations reveal that the ventrolateral neurons, including "morning cells", and dorsolateral neurons, comprising the "evening cells", modulate diurnal oscillations in seizure risk. Pigment-dispersing factor and short neuropeptide F from morning cells increase seizure risk during the day. During this time, morning cell activity increases whole-brain activity. At night, morning cells switch to glycine signaling likely acting on evening cells to decrease seizure risk. Optogenetic inhibition of clock neurons suppresses seizure risk. Our findings reveal an unexpected role for brain clock neurons in modulating daily seizure risk.

articles.titulo: A gut symbiotic bacterium enhances baculovirus resistance in Spodoptera frugiperda by maintaining peritrophic matrix integrity.
articles.autores: Guo L, Jin W, Kang Q, Tong Y, Shi H, Zhang J, Li X, Wang H, Qin Q, Meng Q, Zhang H
articles.resumo_original:
Spodoptera frugiperda is a major agricultural pest worldwide, whereas Spodoptera frugiperda multiple nucleopolyhedrovirus (SfMNPV) serves as an important microbial control agent against this pest. Resident gut bacteria are increasingly recognized as important modulators of insect-pathogen interactions; however, whether and how they influence SfMNPV infection in S. frugiperda remains unclear. We therefore investigated how gut bacteria modulate host resistance to SfMNPV.
Antibiotic-mediated depletion of gut bacteria increased larval susceptibility to SfMNPV. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed that gut bacterial depletion downregulated midgut genes associated with immune defense, digestive functions and peritrophic matrix (PM) maintenance. Among seven culturable midgut bacterial isolates, reinoculation with Glutamicibacter soli significantly enhanced larval resistance to SfMNPV. Pre-feeding with either the G. soli culture supernatant or cell lysis precipitate also increased larval resistance and partially reversed transcriptional changes caused by gut bacterial depletion before viral challenge, including the downregulation of peritrophin-1. RNAi-mediated silencing of peritrophin-1 disrupted PM structure, increased PM permeability, and enhanced larval susceptibility to SfMNPV. Consistently, G. soli reinoculation restored PM integrity impaired by gut bacterial depletion.
These findings identify maintenance of PM integrity as an important mechanism contributing to gut symbiotic bacterium-mediated resistance to SfMNPV. The study advances our understanding of how gut bacteria influence baculovirus infection in insect hosts and provides potential microbial and molecular targets for improving baculovirus-based pest management. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
